title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
author: Daniel Kahneman
blurb: Nobel-winning psychologist Daniel Kahneman explains how our thinking is shaped by two modes. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive. System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful, and also rather lazy. Most of the time System 1 serves us well, but it relies on mental shortcuts that lead to predictable errors. Drawing on decades of research, much of it with his collaborator Amos Tversky, Kahneman shows how we jump to conclusions from limited information, get pulled by irrelevant numbers, trust our judgments more than we should, and fear losses far more than we value equal gains. He also reveals a split between how we experience life and how we remember it. The book doesn't promise to fix our minds. It gives us a vocabulary to recognize when our intuitions are likely to mislead us.

lessons.b: Your thinking runs on a fast, intuitive System 1 and a slow, effortful System 2, and the lazy System 2 often accepts System 1's quick answers without checking them.

lessons.t: What You See Is All There Is
lessons.b: System 1 builds a confident story from whatever information is in front of it and ignores what is missing, so we jump to conclusions from too little evidence.

(fix: Position each end dot exactly on the final point of its path, or remove the end dots if they carry no meaning.)

lessons.b: Anchoring means any number we see first, even an obviously irrelevant one, drags our later estimates toward it.

lessons.t: Why We Trust Our Gut Too Much
lessons.b: We are overconfident because a coherent story feels true, which makes us overrate our predictions and underestimate how long plans will take.
